The association between coffee or caffeine intake and cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) and their risk factors has been extensively researched. However, there has been conflicting evidence. Therefore, the current updated meta-analysis assessed the relationship between coffee or caffeine with CVDs, such as coronary heart diseases (CHDs), myocardial infarction (MI), heart failure (HF), stroke, cardiac arrhythmias, and CVD mortality. Five electronic databases, namely PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus, were extensively searched for all records published between January 2000 and December 2025. Studies were included if they examined the effects of coffee on any CVD and reported the associations in terms of the hazard ratio (HR), relative risk (RR), or odds ratio (OR). Moreover, quality appraisal was conducted using the Newcastle Ottawa Scale for cohort studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute tool for case-control studies. After exclusions, 38 studies involving 2,856,002 participants were reviewed and analyzed. The pooled analysis showed no significant associations between coffee consumption and total CHDs or HF, when comparing the highest and lowest coffee consumption categories (HR: 0.98; p = 0.80 and HR: 1.03; p = 0.62, respectively). In contrast, the pooled results showed a significant positive association between higher coffee consumption and the risk of developing MI (OR: 1.48; p < 0.0001). The pooled analysis also showed an inverse relationship between coffee consumption and stroke or cardiac arrhythmias (HR: 0.89; p = 0.01 and HR: 0.94; p = 0.04, respectively). Furthermore, we observed a non-linear relationship between caffeine intake and CVD mortality among hypertensive patients (HR: 0.68; p = 0.001). Higher coffee intake might increase the risk of MI, but can also offer protective effects against stroke and cardiac arrhythmias. Moreover, higher caffeine intake can reduce the risk of CVD mortality in hypertensive patients. The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12872-026-05693-0. Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world, with research suggesting that over one billion people consume it worldwide [1, 2]. Up to 73% of coffee consumers drink it every day, while only 3.8% drink it once every week [2]. Generally, coffee contains several substances, including lipids, carbohydrates, minerals, vitamins, phenolic compounds, and alkaloids. Caffeine is one of the alkaloids that is naturally present in coffee beans. It is also present in other dietary sources, including tea, cocoa, chocolate bars, and soft drinks. The caffeine content in these dietary sources varies widely, with research showing that it ranges from 4 to 180 mg per 150 ml of coffee, 24 to 50 mg per 150 ml of tea, 15 to 29 mg per 180 ml of cola, 2 to 7 mg per 150 ml of cocoa, and 1 to 36 mg per 28 mg of chocolate [3,4,5]. At low doses, caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, resulting in diuresis, smooth muscle relaxation, cardiac/heart muscle stimulation, and increased gastric secretion in adults [6]. Moreover, caffeine consumption has been recognized to have several positive effects on human health, including the prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and Parkinson’s disease [7, 8]. However, the mechanism behind these benefits is not clearly understood and is not believed to be related to caffeine since decaffeinated coffee also shows similar effects. On the other hand, high doses of caffeine have been shown to contribute to anxiety, nausea, and nervousness [9, 10]. Over the last decade, several meta-analyses have extensively evaluated the association between coffee or caffeine consumption and cardiovascular health. A recently published umbrella review of eleven meta-analyses reported that heavy coffee consumption was associated with an increased risk for cardiovascular diseases. However, further analysis showed that coffee consumption can reduce the risk of dementia and stroke, specifically ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes, by preserving the endothelium and antioxidants [11]. Another comprehensive review examining the relationship between coffee consumption and cardiometabolic health reported that coffee consumption has the potential to prevent stroke but has an ambiguous impact on coronary heart disease. Furthermore, the review noted that moderate coffee consumption (1–5 cups per day) is associated with a low risk of heart failure, but the effects on atrial fibrillation remain inconclusive [12]. Collectively, these reviews suggest that coffee consumption has several cardiovascular health benefits and risks. However, important limitations remain. First, coffee consumption and caffeine intake have been used as interchangeable exposures, despite coffee containing other non-caffeine components. Second, these reviews do not incorporate the most recent cohort studies published in the past few years. Finally, most statistical analyses have focused on composite cardiovascular outcomes, which limits insights condition-specific risks, such as arrhythmias. Therefore, we conducted an updated meta-analysis to comprehensively examine the relationship between coffee or caffeine with a wide range of cardiovascular outcomes.
